# How Many Electrons Fit in a Shell?

<!-- STEP id="capacity" -->
## Each Shell Has a Limit

It is a fair guess that all 11 electrons drop into K, because K has the lowest energy. They cannot, because each shell can hold only a limited number of electrons.

Bohr and Bury gave the limit as **2n²**, where n is the number of the shell. K (n = 1) holds 2, L (n = 2) holds 8 and M (n = 3) holds 18. This was not a guess: the rules were worked out to fit what experiments showed about the elements.

<!-- STEP id="octet-cap" -->
## The Outermost Shell Stops at 8

The second rule is about whichever shell is the outermost one in an atom: it can hold at most 8 electrons. M has room for 18 by the 2n² rule, but in the first eighteen elements M is the outermost shell, so it stops at 8.

<!-- STEP id="order" -->
## Inner Shells Fill First

The third rule gives the order. Electrons fill the shell nearest the nucleus first and then move outward, so L starts to fill only after K is complete, and M only after L is complete.

Now place sodium's 11 electrons yourself. They go 2 in K, 8 in L and 1 in M, which we write as 2,8,1. This list of the electrons in each shell is called the **electronic configuration** of the atom.

**Three rules are enough to place every electron of an atom.**
